name: Belly Down Armbar from Open Guard
description: Master the belly down armbar finish from open guard in BJJ. Learn grip isolation, hip rotation mechanics, and prone finishing details for this high-percentage arm lock.
target_area: Elbow joint hyperextension and ulnar collateral ligament
summary: The Belly Down Armbar from Open Guard isolates a passing opponent's extended arm, swings a leg over their head to lock the armbar, then rotates belly-down so gravity and a hip bridge force a high-percentage elbow hyperextension.
overview:
The belly down armbar finish from open guard is a powerful submission sequence where the guard player isolates an opponent's arm during a passing attempt, establishes the armbar position, and then rotates to a prone orientation to maximize finishing pressure. This technique capitalizes on the open guard player's natural ability to create angles and manipulate distance, converting defensive guard work into an immediate submission threat. The guard player's hip mobility and framing tools provide the foundation for the initial arm isolation that makes the entire sequence possible.

What makes this variant particularly effective from open guard is the element of surprise and the natural arm isolation opportunities arising during grip fighting exchanges. When an opponent reaches forward to establish passing grips or attempts to control the guard player's legs, their arms become vulnerable to being trapped. The rotation to belly-down adds tremendous finishing force because it eliminates the defender's primary escape of stacking and brings gravity to assist the hyperextension. The hitchhiker escape and inward rotation both become significantly more difficult once the attacker commits to the prone position.

This submission demands precise timing during the transition from guard retention to attack, specific hip positioning to clear the opponent's head with the leg, and coordinated arm control throughout the belly-down rotation. It rewards practitioners who develop sensitivity to recognizing when opponents overcommit their weight or extend an arm carelessly during passing attempts, turning those micro-errors into fight-ending submissions.

injury_risks.injury: Elbow hyperextension with ligament damage to the ulnar collateral ligament
Elbow joint capsule sprain or partial tear from forced extension
Biceps tendon strain or partial tear from resisting extension under load
Distal humerus stress fracture from sustained pressure against locked elbow

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive. The belly down position creates significant mechanical advantage that can damage the elbow extremely quickly. Apply extension gradually and allow adequate time for the tap. Never jerk or spike the arm. The prone position amplifies force beyond what most practitioners expect.
tap_signals: Verbal tap saying 'tap' or any distress vocalization
Physical hand tap on partner, mat, or own body
Physical foot tap on mat with either leg
Any screaming, grunting, or unusual vocalization indicating distress
release_protocol: Release immediately upon any tap signal without waiting for confirmation or repetition
If in doubt whether a tap occurred, release immediately — the position can be re-established safely
Release extension pressure first by lowering the wrist, then release knee squeeze, then disengage completely
Monitor training partner's arm mobility after release and check for signs of injury before continuing
training_restrictions: Beginners should practice mechanics at 50% pressure maximum until transition control is consistent
Always apply extension slowly in training — never jerk or spike the arm during the belly down finish
Do not apply this technique on training partners with known elbow injuries or recent arm submissions
Practice the transition rotation separately from the finishing pressure until both components are reliable

attacker.name: Belly Down Armbar from Open Guard Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to attack the belly down armbar finish from open guard. Step-by-step grip isolation, hip angle creation, prone rotation mechanics, and progressive finishing pressure.
attacker.overview: Executing the belly down armbar finish from open guard requires reading your opponent's passing intentions and converting their forward pressure into an arm isolation opportunity. The key attacking sequence involves securing wrist control with a 2-on-1 grip, cutting a sharp hip angle to create perpendicular alignment, swinging the far leg over the head while maintaining arm tension, and then committing fully to the belly-down rotation. The prone finishing position generates substantial mechanical advantage through hip bridge pressure against the hyperextended elbow, making this one of the most secure armbar finishes available from guard. Success depends on precise timing during the transition from guard retention to offensive attack.
key_principles: Control the wrist with a 2-on-1 grip before committing to the hip cut — arm isolation is the foundation of the entire attack sequence
Create a sharp perpendicular angle with your hips relative to the opponent's torso before swinging the leg over their head
Maintain constant tension on the trapped arm throughout the rotation — any slack allows the defender to retract the elbow
Commit fully to the belly-down rotation once the leg clears the head — half-rotations create escape windows
Squeeze knees together tightly around the upper arm to prevent the defender from extracting the elbow at any stage
Use your chest and both hands to pin the wrist against your sternum during the prone finish for maximum control
setup_requirements: Establish a dominant 2-on-1 grip on the opponent's wrist or sleeve using pistol grip and cross-grip configuration
Create a perpendicular angle by hip escaping to align your body at 90 degrees to the opponent's centerline
Position your near-side foot on the opponent's hip as a frame to control distance and prevent them from closing the gap
Break the opponent's posture enough to clear a path for your far leg to swing over their head without obstruction
Confirm the elbow orientation — the thumb side of the trapped arm must face your hips for the hyperextension mechanics to function

execution_steps.description: From open guard, identify when the opponent extends an arm to establish a passing grip. Secure their wrist with both hands using a pistol grip and cross-grip combination, pulling their arm across your centerline to break their posture alignment and create the initial isolation.
execution_steps.timing: 0-3 seconds, must be immediate on arm extension

execution_steps.description: Execute a hip escape away from the trapped arm side, rotating your body to create a perpendicular angle to the opponent's torso. Plant your near-side foot firmly on their hip to maintain distance control and prevent them from driving forward to stack or recover posture.
execution_steps.timing: 1-2 seconds, immediately after securing the grip

execution_steps.action: Swing the leg over the head
execution_steps.description: Swing your far-side leg over the opponent's head and face, hooking behind their neck or across their shoulder line. Keep your near-side leg tight against their body with your knee clamped against their ribcage to prevent them from posturing up or pulling their arm free.

Pinch both knees tightly together around the opponent's upper arm, trapping the bicep between your thighs. Pull the wrist firmly to your chest with both hands, ensuring the thumb side of their hand faces upward toward the ceiling and the elbow joint is aligned against your hip line for extension.

Begin rotating toward the thumb side of the trapped arm by turning your shoulders and hips in a unified motion. Maintain the knee squeeze and wrist control throughout the rotation, using the momentum of the turn to prevent the opponent from following your movement and creating escape angles.

Finish the full belly-down rotation so your chest faces the mat. Pull the trapped wrist tight against your sternum with both hands. Walk your feet closer to your hips to establish a strong bridge base, keeping your toes planted and your core braced for the finishing pressure application.
execution_steps.timing: 1-2 seconds to settle into final position

execution_steps.description: With your body prone and hips elevated, bridge upward gradually into the back of the opponent's elbow while maintaining chest-to-wrist contact. Make micro-adjustments by raising your hips in small increments. Monitor for the tap signal constantly — the mechanical advantage is extreme and minimal movement creates significant extension pressure on the elbow joint.

common_counters.counter: Defender stacks forward immediately upon feeling arm isolation, driving weight onto the guard player to compress the attacking structure
common_counters.your_response: Maintain the foot on hip as a frame and use it to push them back while simultaneously accelerating the hip cut angle — the stack loses effectiveness once you achieve perpendicular alignment

common_counters.counter: Defender retracts the trapped arm by bending the elbow and pulling it toward their chest before the leg clears their head
common_counters.your_response: Switch to an omoplata or triangle attempt by using the momentum and angle already established — the arm retraction creates space for these alternative attacks from the same hip angle

common_counters.counter: Defender postures aggressively and stands tall to strip the guard player's feet off their hips and create distance
common_counters.your_response: Follow their upward movement by elevating your hips and maintaining wrist control — their standing posture actually creates better angles for the leg to swing over the head

common_counters.counter: Defender turns into the armbar during the belly-down rotation, following the rotation direction to relieve elbow pressure and work to pass
common_counters.your_response: Accelerate the rotation and clamp knees tighter — if they begin to come on top, transition to standard face-up armbar finish with your far heel across their chest and hips raised

common_errors.error: Attempting the armbar without first isolating the arm with a secure 2-on-1 grip
common_errors.consequence: Opponent easily retracts their arm and reestablishes passing posture, wasting energy and revealing your attacking intention prematurely
common_errors.correction: Always establish firm wrist control with both hands before beginning the hip cut — the grip is the anchor for the entire submission sequence

common_errors.error: Cutting the hip angle too shallow, remaining nearly parallel to the opponent's torso
common_errors.consequence: Far leg cannot clear the head for the armbar position, and the opponent can easily drive forward to smash and flatten the guard
common_errors.correction: Hip escape aggressively to create a full perpendicular angle — your hips should point at the ceiling relative to the opponent's centerline

common_errors.error: Failing to maintain knee squeeze during the belly-down rotation transition
common_errors.consequence: Opponent extracts their arm during the rotation, escaping the submission before the prone finishing position is established
common_errors.correction: Squeeze knees together as the highest priority throughout the rotation — pinching the upper arm with your inner thighs is a non-negotiable checkpoint at every stage

common_errors.error: Rotating to belly-down without the wrist secured firmly against the chest
common_errors.consequence: The arm slips free during rotation because there is no anchor point, and the opponent recovers posture and passing position
common_errors.correction: Pin the wrist to your sternum with both hands before and during the rotation — the wrist-to-chest connection must remain constant throughout the entire turn

common_errors.error: Applying the finish with a jerking or explosive hip motion rather than progressive pressure
common_errors.consequence: Risk of serious elbow injury to training partner and potential disqualification in competition for dangerous submission application
common_errors.correction: Bridge hips upward slowly and progressively — the belly-down position generates enormous force so even small hip movements create significant elbow extension pressure

common_errors.error: Leaving the near-side leg loose against the opponent's body instead of clamping tightly against their ribcage
common_errors.consequence: Opponent creates space to posture up, stack forward, or spin their body to escape the armbar position before the belly-down rotation begins
common_errors.correction: Keep the near-side knee pinched against the opponent's ribcage throughout setup and transition to prevent any space creation or posture recovery

training_progressions.focus: Arm isolation and hip angle from open guard
training_progressions.description: Partner extends arm from combat base while you practice the 2-on-1 grip and hip escape to perpendicular angle. No resistance. Focus on the grip-to-angle connection at slow speed until the movement pattern becomes automatic.

training_progressions.focus: Clearing the leg over the head and establishing armbar control
training_progressions.description: From the established hip angle, practice swinging the far leg over the partner's head and securing the knee squeeze. Partner holds position stationary. Focus on smooth leg trajectory and immediate clamp upon landing.

training_progressions.focus: Full rotation while maintaining arm control under light resistance
training_progressions.description: Practice the complete belly-down rotation from the armbar position with light partner resistance on arm retraction. Focus on maintaining wrist-to-chest contact and knee squeeze throughout the entire turning motion.

training_progressions.focus: Complete sequence against increasing defensive intensity
training_progressions.description: Execute the full submission chain from open guard against 50-75% resistance. Partner attempts realistic counters including stacking, arm retraction, and posturing. Apply finish with controlled progressive pressure only.

training_progressions.focus: Integration into live sparring from open guard
training_progressions.description: Begin from open guard in positional sparring. Attacker works for the belly down armbar while defender attempts normal passing sequences. Focus on recognizing live opportunities and timing the arm isolation correctly against unpredictable movement.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structure does the belly down armbar finish primarily attack?
flashcards.answer: The belly down armbar finish targets the elbow joint by hyperextending it beyond its natural range of motion. Specifically, it attacks the ulnar collateral ligament and the joint capsule of the elbow, applying pressure against the natural hinge direction. The belly-down position amplifies this force because hip bridge pressure acts directly against the posterior aspect of the extended elbow, creating substantial mechanical advantage.

flashcards.question: What grip configuration should you establish before initiating the hip cut from open guard?
flashcards.answer: Secure a 2-on-1 grip on the opponent's wrist using a pistol grip with your near hand and a cross-grip or C-grip with your far hand. Both hands must control the wrist before the hip escape begins, because the grip is the anchor for maintaining arm isolation throughout the entire sequence from hip cut through belly-down rotation. Without this dual wrist control, the opponent can retract the arm during any phase of the attack.

flashcards.question: Why is the belly-down rotation considered the point of no escape for the defender?
flashcards.answer: Once the attacker completes the belly-down rotation with knees squeezed and wrist pinned to the chest, the defender loses their primary escape options. They cannot stack because the attacker is prone. The hitchhiker escape becomes extremely difficult because the rotation direction has already moved past the escape window. The mechanical advantage of the hip bridge from the prone position makes even very small upward movements generate significant hyperextension pressure on the elbow joint.

flashcards.question: How should you apply finishing pressure to prevent injury during training?
flashcards.answer: Apply the hip bridge slowly and progressively, raising your hips in small increments while constantly monitoring for the tap. The belly-down position generates far more force than a standard face-up armbar, so the margin between submission pressure and injury is significantly smaller. Never jerk or spike the hips upward. Allow the training partner adequate time to recognize the submission and tap before increasing pressure further. If uncertain, pause rather than increase force.

flashcards.question: Your opponent starts retracting their arm as you initiate the hip angle — what adjustment prevents escape?
flashcards.answer: If the arm retraction happens early before the leg is over the head, immediately transition to an omoplata or triangle attempt using the momentum and perpendicular angle you have already created. Do not chase the retracting arm aggressively as this exposes you to being stacked. The same hip angle that sets up the armbar creates excellent entry angles for omoplata and triangle attacks, making the arm retraction a trigger for chain attacks rather than a failed sequence.

flashcards.question: What immediate action must you take when your training partner taps during the belly down finish?
flashcards.answer: Release all hip bridge pressure immediately by lowering your hips flat to the mat. Then release the wrist grip and open your knees to free the arm completely. Do not hold the position even momentarily after the tap signal. The extreme mechanical advantage of the prone position means that continued pressure for even a fraction of a second after the tap can cause significant elbow ligament damage that may require months of rehabilitation.

flashcards.question: Your opponent begins turning into you during the belly-down rotation to relieve pressure — what adjustment completes the finish?
flashcards.answer: If the opponent follows your rotation, accelerate the turn and tighten the knee squeeze to prevent them from fully rotating with you. If they manage to come to their side, transition to a standard face-up armbar by placing your far heel across their chest and raising your hips. The key is recognizing whether to complete the belly-down finish or transition to the standard armbar based on how far the defender follows the rotation direction.

flashcards.question: What control checkpoints must be confirmed before committing to the belly-down rotation?
flashcards.answer: Three checkpoints must be confirmed: first, the wrist is pinned firmly against your chest with both hands maintaining the 2-on-1 grip. Second, both knees are squeezing tightly around the opponent's upper arm with no gap between your thighs and their bicep. Third, the opponent's posture is broken enough that they cannot stack forward during the rotation. Missing any one of these checkpoints during the rotation creates an escape window that experienced defenders will exploit.

defender.name: Belly Down Armbar from Open Guard Defender
defender.description: Learn to defend and escape the belly down armbar finish from open guard. Recognition cues, early grip defense, escape timing, and safe tap protocols for this dangerous arm lock.
defender.overview: Defending the belly down armbar finish from open guard requires recognizing the early stages of arm isolation before the attacker can establish the full armbar position. Once the attacker begins the belly-down rotation, escape options diminish rapidly due to the extreme mechanical advantage of the prone finishing position. Successful defense prioritizes keeping elbows tight during passing, immediately addressing any 2-on-1 grip situations, and understanding that the critical defensive window closes the moment the attacker's leg clears your head. Early recognition and posture maintenance are far more effective than late-stage escape attempts against this particular finish. Knowing when to tap is equally important as knowing how to escape, because the prone armbar generates force that can cause injury faster than most practitioners expect.
key_principles: Keep elbows tight to your body during all open guard passing attempts — extended arms are the primary vulnerability that enables this attack
Recognize 2-on-1 grip situations immediately and strip the grip before the attacker can establish the perpendicular hip angle
Maintain upright posture throughout passing sequences — broken posture enables the attacker's leg to swing over your head
React to the attacker's hip escape by driving forward immediately — the perpendicular angle is the critical setup for the entire sequence
If the armbar position is established, prioritize stacking before the belly-down rotation begins — once the attacker is prone, escape difficulty increases dramatically
Tap early and decisively when caught in the completed belly-down position — the mechanical advantage is extreme and injury onset is rapid
recognition_cues: Opponent secures 2-on-1 or cross-grip wrist control on your extended arm while you are passing their open guard
Guard player executes a sharp hip escape creating a perpendicular angle to your body while maintaining firm wrist control with both hands
Far leg begins swinging upward toward your head and face while the near-side knee clamps against your ribcage to prevent posture recovery
Guard player's hips begin rotating toward the mat as they initiate the belly-down turn with your arm trapped between their knees

defensive_options.action: Strip the 2-on-1 grip immediately using a circular wrist extraction before the hip angle is established
defensive_options.when_to_use: As soon as you feel both of the opponent's hands controlling your wrist or sleeve during open guard passing
defensive_options.if_successful: Return to neutral open guard passing position with both arms free and guard player's attack reset
defensive_options.risk: If the grip strip fails, you may extend your arm further and create a better isolation angle for the attacker

defensive_options.action: Drive forward with heavy shoulder pressure to stack the guard player before the belly-down rotation begins
defensive_options.when_to_use: After the armbar position is partially established but before the attacker begins turning prone — the window is narrow
defensive_options.if_successful: Collapse the armbar structure, compress the guard player, and work to extract the arm to return to passing position
defensive_options.risk: If the attacker has already begun rotating, driving forward can actually accelerate the hyperextension rather than relieve it

defensive_options.action: Turn into the armbar rotation direction and come to your knees to relieve elbow pressure while working to pass
defensive_options.when_to_use: During the belly-down rotation as the attacker turns — you must follow the same rotation direction they are turning
defensive_options.if_successful: Relieve the elbow extension pressure by following the rotation and work to extract the arm while advancing to a top position
defensive_options.risk: If the attacker clamps knees tighter and accelerates the turn, you may be unable to keep pace and get caught in a deeper prone finish

escape_paths: Hitchhiker escape — straighten the trapped arm and rotate your thumb toward the mat, turning your body in the same direction to slip the elbow past the attacker's hip line before the belly-down rotation completes
Stack and retract — drive your weight forward onto the guard player while bending the trapped elbow and pulling it toward your centerline, collapsing the space needed for the leg to clear your head

Follow the rotation — turn your body in the same direction as the attacker's belly-down rotation, coming to your knees to relieve elbow pressure and working to extract the arm while establishing a top passing position

favorable_outcomes.how: Follow the belly-down rotation direction to relieve elbow pressure, extract your arm while coming to your knees, and establish a passing position against the guard player's closed guard recovery

common_errors.error: Leaving the arm extended during open guard passing without awareness of arm isolation threats
common_errors.consequence: Opponent easily secures 2-on-1 control and the entire submission chain becomes available before you recognize the danger
common_errors.correction: Keep elbows bent and close to your body when reaching for passing grips — retract immediately if you feel both hands controlling your wrist

common_errors.error: Attempting to escape by pulling the arm straight backward once the legs are in armbar position
common_errors.consequence: Pulling backward extends the arm further and makes the belly-down rotation easier for the attacker by straightening the elbow
common_errors.correction: Drive forward to stack or turn into the armbar direction — backward pulling plays directly into the hyperextension mechanics of the submission

common_errors.error: Delaying the tap when caught in the completed belly-down position hoping to find a late escape
common_errors.consequence: The extreme mechanical advantage of the prone position means elbow damage can occur within seconds — late taps frequently result in ligament injuries requiring months of recovery
common_errors.correction: Tap immediately and decisively when the belly-down rotation completes and you feel extension pressure — this position has a very narrow margin between pressure and structural damage

common_errors.error: Trying to use bicep strength to bend the arm against the attacker's hip bridge from the belly-down position
common_errors.consequence: The hip bridge force vastly exceeds what the bicep can resist, leading to rapid elbow hyperextension or bicep tendon strain under extreme load
common_errors.correction: Focus on positional escapes like the hitchhiker or following the rotation rather than attempting to muscle through the extension pressure with arm strength alone

flashcards.question: How do you recognize that a belly down armbar finish is being set up from open guard?
flashcards.answer: The primary recognition cues are the opponent securing 2-on-1 wrist control followed by a sharp hip escape to create a perpendicular angle to your body. When you feel both hands on your wrist and see their hips turning away from you, you are in the initial stages of the attack. Additional cues include the far leg beginning to rise toward your head. The earlier you identify these signs, the more escape options remain available to you.

flashcards.question: When should you tap to a belly down armbar finish to prevent injury?
flashcards.answer: Tap immediately when you feel extension pressure on your elbow after the attacker has completed the belly-down rotation. The prone position generates extreme mechanical advantage, and the window between feeling pressure and sustaining ligament damage is very small compared to standard armbars. Do not wait to see if you can still escape once the prone position is fully established — tap at the first sign of progressive elbow extension from the completed belly-down position.

flashcards.question: What defensive options are available before versus after the belly-down rotation completes?
flashcards.answer: Before the rotation, you can strip the 2-on-1 grip, stack the guard player forward, posture aggressively to prevent the leg from crossing your head, or retract the arm by bending the elbow toward your chest. After the rotation completes, options narrow dramatically to the hitchhiker escape and following the rotation to relieve pressure. The belly-down rotation is the critical threshold — defense before it is proactive and varied, defense after it is reactive and severely limited.

flashcards.question: Why is pulling your arm straight backward the wrong defensive response when caught in this armbar?
flashcards.answer: Pulling backward extends the arm further away from your body, which is exactly what the attacker needs — it straightens the elbow joint and creates more space for the belly-down finish to generate maximum hyperextension force. The correct response is to drive forward to collapse the space between you and the guard player, or turn into the submission direction to relieve the extension angle. Backward pulling also shifts your weight away from the attacker, removing any stacking pressure that could compress their attacking structure.

training_progressions.focus: Identifying early attack cues during open guard passing
training_progressions.description: Partner works the arm isolation and hip angle at slow speed while you practice identifying the 2-on-1 grip and perpendicular hip escape. No escape attempts yet — focus purely on reading when the attack sequence begins and verbalizing the recognition cues.

training_progressions.focus: Grip stripping and posture maintenance before armbar establishes
training_progressions.description: Partner attempts the full belly down armbar setup from open guard at 50% speed. Practice stripping the 2-on-1 grip with circular wrist extraction, maintaining upright posture, and retracting the arm before the leg clears the head. Reset positions if the armbar is fully established.

training_progressions.focus: Escaping established positions and recognizing safe tap windows
training_progressions.description: Begin with the attacker already in armbar position before belly-down rotation. Practice the hitchhiker escape, stack defense, and following the rotation direction. Critically, practice recognizing when escape is no longer viable and tapping decisively rather than fighting a fully locked belly-down position.

training_progressions.focus: Integrating defense into live open guard passing situations
training_progressions.description: Positional sparring from open guard top where the bottom player specifically hunts the belly down armbar. Practice maintaining safe arm positioning during passing while recognizing and defending the attack chain in live conditions with full resistance.
